en: Idle cranes

A crane does useful work only while it is moving a load. With chains and slings, the crane waits while the rigging is fitted, checked and removed. On a busy bay, one slow lift holds up the next job in the queue.
A Maxx lifter stays on the crane hook between lifts.
A magnetic lifter stays on the hook. It is set on the load and switched on with one turn of the handle. The crane spends more of each hour lifting.
Extra labour
A sling lift on a large plate often needs a second person to fit the slings and guide the load. That person is tied to the crane for every lift.
With a magnetic lifter, one operator can attach, lift and release the load. The second person can do other work.
Tired crews

Chains are heavy. Dragging them to the load, lifting them over plate edges and pulling slings out from under a load is hard physical work. By the end of a shift, the crew is slower. Tired people also make more mistakes.
A lifter needs one hand on the lever. The effort is small on every lift, so the operator stays fresh through the shift.
Slings and chains wear out

Slings fray and cut on sharp edges. Chains stretch and their links wear. All lifting gear has to be inspected, tagged and replaced when it is damaged. A shop that lifts plates of many sizes also needs many lengths and ratings, and each one has to be stored and tracked.
SMAG lifters use neodymium magnets and need no power and no maintenance. One lifter covers every flat or round load within its rating.
Damage to finished steel
Chains dent edges and wire rope marks surfaces. On ground plate, machined parts or coated steel, a mark can mean rework or a rejected part. Padding the load takes more time on every lift.
The base of a magnetic lifter is flat and smooth. It leaves no mark on a finished surface.
Accidents stop work

A slipped sling or a trapped hand can injure a person. It also stops the bay. Work halts while the injured person is cared for, the area is made safe and the cause is found. A serious incident can close a site for days.

With a magnetic lifter, nobody reaches under the load to fit or release it. The handle locks in the on position, and there is no power supply to fail. Our guide on {1}safer lifting{/1} covers this in more detail.
Adding it up

None of these costs shows on the invoice for the lifting gear. Together they add up over every shift. For a side by side look at the two methods, see {1}magnetic lifters compared with chains and slings{/1}

How Black Powder Forms in Pipelines | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / How Black Powder Forms in Pipelines
Pipeline guide

Black powder is a common problem in steel pipelines. It forms in gas, oil, petrochemical and aviation fuel lines. It is fine iron sulphide and iron oxide, made by corrosion of the pipe wall. The particles are very small, often less than a micron across. They can travel as a dry powder, stay suspended in a liquid, or settle as a black sludge.
How does black powder form?
Carbon steel pipe corrodes when certain substances are present in the flow. The main ones are:
Rust and iron sulphide form on the wall
Particles break off and travel with the flow
Magnetic filter holds the black powder
Clean flow
Black powder forms on the pipe wall, travels with the flow and is held in a magnetic filter.
water
oxygen
hydrogen sulphide
carbon dioxide
Together they attack the inside of the pipe. Iron from the wall reacts to form iron sulphide and iron oxide. These compounds break away from the wall as fine particles and join the flow.
The process is slow. Over months and years, an untreated line can collect a large amount of black powder. The flow also rubs against the pipe wall, and this erosion adds more particles.
Why is black powder a problem?
{1}It narrows the pipe.{/1} Black powder settles along the pipe and at low points. The open bore gets smaller, so flow and pressure fall. Operators then have to scrape or pig the line to clear it.

{1}It wears equipment.{/1} The particles are hard and abrasive. They wear the pipe wall and damage compressors, pumps, valves and burner nozzles. They can also block small passages. A meter with black powder in it can give false readings.

{1}It blocks barrier filters.{/1} Many lines use cartridge or barrier filters to catch black powder. The fine particles soon block them. Each blocked filter has to be removed, replaced and disposed of. This brings a steady cost in filter elements, labour and waste handling.
{1}It is hazardous to handle.{/1} Dry iron sulphide can catch fire on contact with air. Used filters and collected powder need careful handling and must be disposed of as hazardous waste.
How does a magnetic filter help?

Black powder is an iron compound, so a magnet holds it. A magnetic pipeline filter places strong neodymium rods in the flow. As gas or liquid passes the rods, the particles collect on them. The clean flow carries on down the line.

A magnetic filter has no filter element to block or replace. The flow path stays open as the rods load, so pressure stays steady between cleans. To clean the filter, the rods are lifted out and wiped. The collected powder is removed in one place, in a controlled way.
With a magnetic filter upstream, barrier filters further down the line block less often. Compressors, pumps, valves and meters see less abrasive wear.
Where do the filters go?
Filters can be fitted at many points in the system:
Upstream, at wellhead control, heating and cooling systems and pressure reduction.
Midstream, in filtration trains, gas gathering stations and pig receiving stations.
Downstream, at refinery inlets and storage.
Ahead of compressors, meters and control valves anywhere in the line.
Sizing a filter

To size a filter, we need the line size, the operating pressure, the flow rate and the type of contamination you see. The connection type matters too, because each unit is made to fit the existing pipework.

How Magnetic Filtration Works | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / How Magnetic Filtration Works
Filtration guide

Magnetic filtration removes iron and steel particles from a liquid with a magnet. The liquid flows around magnetic rods. The particles are pulled onto the rods and stay there. The clean liquid carries on to the machine or the next stage of the process.
It is used for machine coolant, cutting fluid, neat oil, hydraulic oil, wash liquid and many process liquids.
What is inside the filter?
A magnetic filter has two main parts: a housing and a set of magnetic rods.
Magnetic rods of this kind sit inside the filter housing.
The housing is a sealed body with an inlet and an outlet. It fits into the pipe that carries the liquid. The rods hang inside the housing, in the path of the flow.

Each rod is a sealed stainless steel tube. Inside the tube are strong neodymium magnets with steel pole pieces between them. The pole pieces concentrate the magnetic field at the surface of the tube. The tube is welded and watertight, so the liquid never touches the magnets.
How are the particles caught?
Iron and steel are ferrous metals. A magnet attracts them.
Liquid with iron particles
Magnetic rods hold the iron
Sealed housing
Lid lifts out with
the rods for cleaning
Liquid flows around the magnetic rods. Iron particles are pulled onto the rods and the clean liquid flows on.

As the liquid passes the rods, each ferrous particle feels a pull towards the nearest rod. The pull is strongest close to the rod surface. A particle that comes close enough is drawn onto the tube and held there. The flow is not strong enough to wash it off.

Size does not decide what is caught. A large chip and a very fine grinding particle are both ferrous, so both are attracted. This is why a magnetic filter can hold the fine wear particles that pass through a paper or bag filter. The page on {1}magnetic filters compared with other filters{/1} sets out the differences in full.
Some non-magnetic dirt is also held. It gets trapped in the layer of iron that builds up on the rods. The amount depends on the liquid and the process.
What decides how well it works?

{1}Magnetic strength.{/1} Strength at the rod surface is measured in gauss. A stronger rod reaches further into the flow and holds finer particles. SMAG rods are made in four strengths, from 7,000 gauss up to 13,500 gauss.

{1}Time near the rods.{/1} The liquid must pass close to the rods and slowly enough for the particles to be drawn out. The housing is sized to the flow rate for this reason. The rods are spaced so that the liquid cannot find a path that avoids them.
